content: Evidence from systematic reviews of observational studies has suggested that hormone therapy might reduce the incidence of cardiovascular disease events in post-menopausal women. However, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have shown inconsistent results. This updated Cochrane review aimed to evaluate the effects of hormone therapy on preventing cardiovascular disease in post-menopausal women, distinguishing between its use for primary and secondary prevention. Additionally, the review explored whether the timing of treatment initiation relative to menopause (less than 10 years versus 10 or more years) or the duration of treatment influenced outcomes. The review included 19 RCTs involving a total of 40,410 post-menopausal women. The overall quality of the studies was good, with a low risk of bias. The findings were largely influenced by the three largest trials. High-quality evidence demonstrated that hormone therapy, whether used for primary or secondary prevention, did not reduce all-cause mortality, cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, angina, or the need for revascularization. However, hormone therapy was associated with an increased risk of stroke (relative risk [RR] 1.24, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.10 to 1.41), venous thromboembolic events (RR 1.92, 95% CI 1.36 to 2.69), and pulmonary embolism (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.32 to 2.48) compared to placebo. The absolute risk increase for stroke was 6 per 1,000 women, with a number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) of 165 over a mean follow-up of 4.21 years (range: 2.0 to 7.1 years). For venous thromboembolism, the absolute risk increase was 8 per 1,000 women (NNTH = 118; mean follow-up: 5.95 years, range: 1.0 to 7.1 years). For pulmonary embolism, the absolute risk increase was 4 per 1,000 women (NNTH = 242; mean follow-up: 3.13 years, range: 1.0 to 7.1 years). Subgroup analyses revealed that the timing of hormone therapy initiation relative to menopause influenced outcomes. Women who started hormone therapy less than 10 years after menopause experienced lower mortality (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.95) and a reduced risk of coronary heart disease (a composite of cardiovascular death and non-fatal myocardial infarction) (RR 0.52, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.96). However, this group still faced an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.73). There was no strong evidence of an increased risk of stroke in this subgroup. In contrast, women who initiated hormone therapy more than 10 years after menopause showed no significant reduction in mortality or coronary heart disease risk. However, they had an increased risk of stroke (RR 1.21, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.38) and venous thromboembolism (RR 1.96, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.80). In conclusion, the findings provide robust evidence that hormone therapy in post-menopausal women, whether for primary or secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease, offers little to no benefit and increases the risk of stroke and venous thromboembolic events. The timing of therapy initiation relative to menopause appears to influence some outcomes, but the risks associated with hormone therapy remain significant.
